lines.text: Moreover we are not speaking of those outside our own
circle, outside the Church and the Christian faith. No, we
all belong integrally to modern life and are all subject to this
temptation.
The declaration that God is Judge calls our attention to
the fact that all the phenomena of life are ambiguous and
hence sources of temptation, the fact that we may use them
for good or lose our souls to them. But we do in fact lose our
souls to them if we believe them to be unequivocal, thus
ceasing to feel their power to tempt and lead astray. We owe
an account as to what we make of them. This however
applies above all to ourselves, to the energies and impulses,
the gifts and the passions of our inner being. These latter are
by no means unequivocal, and not everything that springs
from the instincts of blood and nature is good. Primitive man
is aware of the frailty and dubiety of his being, for he is
aware of its dangers and does not suppose that he is master
of himself. The German poet too knows this: "Ah! how little
we know ourselves, for a divine force lives and moves within
us" (Hölderlin). In a very popular book of our time, the
Majorin of Ernst Wiechert, the author shows most con-
vincingly and vividly that men know themselves so little and
then are terrified at themselves when unsuspected forces
burst forth from the inner heart of their lives.
But modern man thinks he knows himself, or he lives as if
he did. He can do this only because he has forgotten the
truth: "In Him we live and move and have our being."
For this word warns him that he lives his life before the
eyes of a judge, to whom he is always responsible, always
transparent. "Whither shall I go from Thy Spirit, or whither
shall I flee from Thy presence?"
Modern man supposes that he is not ambivalent in the
impulses and stirrings of his blood. How seldom now are we
terrified at ourselves, how seldom do we shudder to con-
template our own thoughts and deeds! We are rather
accustomed to praise and extol our thoughts and deeds
when they lead to achievements which are visible to all.
1 E. T. The Baroness, 1936.
